note: WHO DECIDES WHAT: the one declaration of the boundary between the deterministic rule layer
(packages/judge/src/rules.ts) and the trained scorer's per-subtype heads.
It is a FILE, and language-neutral, because two programs need this same fact and they are not
written in the same language: score-rules.ts gates the rule layer against real captures, and
train-screenreader-model.py decides which heads may block a release. It was declared twice -- a
TypeScript array and a Python frozenset -- and by the time anyone compared them they had already
drifted apart in BOTH directions:
- the TypeScript list carried `4.1.2:unnamed-form-field`, a key that exists in no record
- the Python set omitted the 115 unnamed-form-field records entirely, because it keyed on the
corpus vocabulary and the TypeScript keyed on a criterion it minted itself
Secure by Design 12.5 names this exactly: DRY is about duplicated KNOWLEDGE, not duplicated text.
Two encodings of one business rule 'evolve inconsistently', and the duplication is invisible to a
text-duplication tool because the two encodings do not look alike. That is what happened here.
## The key is the corpus's own subtype vocabulary
`target.subtypes` in the dataset export -- `1.1.1:missing-alt`, `4.1.2:unnamed-control` -- and NOT
`provenance.subtype`, which is a case-family name and is ambiguous: `regex` is three different
subtypes under 2.4.4, 2.4.6 and 4.1.2. The model's heads are named after this vocabulary and the
scorer report keys on it, so making the rule gate speak it too means one vocabulary, not two.
## `reportsAs` exists because the two layers disagree, defensibly
The corpus labels an unnamed form field `3.3.2:unnamed-form-field` (a missing label); the rule
reported it under 4.1.2 alone until ADR 0017; it now reports BOTH, because both are true.
Declaring the mapping is the only way the gate can check the rule fired at all -- and previously
this fact lived in a Python comment that the TypeScript side could not see, which is why the
TypeScript side invented a key for it.
## Absence means the model decides it
Only the exceptions are listed. A subtype missing from this file is the scorer's, and the gate
asserts the rules never fire its criterion on it -- so a new subtype the rules DO touch fails
loudly rather than being silently adopted.

1.1.1:filename-alt.note: An exact-absence case: alt text that is a filename is no alternative at all.

1.1.1:missing-alt.note: An exact-absence case. NVDA's 'unlabeled' prefix is nondeterministic, and keying on it once cost 3 of 88 -- the defect that made this gate exist.

3.3.2:placeholder-only.note: NOT WITNESSABLE by a screen reader, and this is a property of the criterion rather than a gap in our evidence. When a field has no label the browser uses the placeholder as its accessible name, so NVDA announces it exactly as it announces a real label: `<input placeholder="Email address">` and `<label>Email address</label><input>` both speak "Email address, edit". The difference exists only in the DOM, which is axe-core's layer -- this tool runs alongside it, not instead of it. Measured 2026-08-23: the head had no placeholder feature at all, weighted the encoder 598.9 against 9.26 for every document feature combined, and had learned the corpus's placeholder wording -- it fired on 4 of the 6 clean pages containing "Example value" and 0 of the 34 without. Eight false accusations on conformant pages. See ADR 0018.

3.3.2:unnamed-form-field.note: 3.3.2 since 2026-08-23 (ADR 0017). The rule ALSO reports 4.1.2 for this evidence -- an unnamed input fails both -- and `4.1.2:unnamed-control` carries that side. What `reportsAs` decides is whether the rule SUBSTITUTES for this head, and it now does. While this said 4.1.2 the trainer kept a head for a subtype the rules already decided 115/115, because nothing emitted the criterion the corpus labels, and that head produced eight false accusations on conformant form pages. These records also carry `4.1.2:missing-role`, so the gate must credit that subtype for them too or its boundary reads as ragged.

4.1.2:unnamed-control.note: An exact-absence case: a control announced with a role and no name -- an icon button or a text input, one failure, one subtype. It was `4.1.2:regex`, a key naming the MATCHER rather than the failure, while the 115 unlabelled-field records sat in `4.1.2:missing-role`, the head for the opposite failure.

note: NOBODY decides this one, and saying so out loud is the whole point of the entry.
A role-less `<div onclick>` styled as a button. The screen reader cannot perceive it -- that IS
the failure -- so to NVDA a page with a fake button and a page with no button are the same page.
All 74 records announce `formFields: []` and `controls: []`, and so do 437 of the 1,003
conformant records, because a page about images or tables has no controls either.
Measured both ways before giving up on it: instance-max pooling gives precision 1.000 at recall
0.824 (13 misses), document-mean gives recall 1.000 at precision 0.782 (21 false accusations on
conformant pages, on a corpus far cleaner than the web). So the records are excluded from the
model -- see MODEL_EXCLUDED_SUBTYPES, whose reason string is exactly 'not inferable from
screen-reader output alone'.
This is a statement about the EVIDENCE, not a permanent verdict. 'This element responds to
clicks, exposes no role, and cannot be reached by keyboard' is deterministic and obtainable over
the CDP socket the capture already opens; once captured it belongs to the rule layer, which is
exact on 1,003 conformant records. That needs a CAPTURE_PROTOCOL_VERSION bump and a recapture.
Until then 4.1.2 is PARTIALLY covered, and a consumer has to be able to learn that from
somewhere. `rules:score` asserts these records are absent from the export -- the inverse of the
check it applies to every other entry -- so the exclusion cannot quietly stop working.
A total failure, and the only criterion here where the rule outranks everything else on the
report: WCAG 5.2.5 makes 2.1.2 non-interference, so a keyboard user who cannot leave a control
cannot use the rest of the page at all. Deterministic because the evidence is arithmetic rather
than wording -- Tab repeated the same stop, and focus reached fewer controls than the form-field
sweep found. Measured on this case: bad stops at 3 of 5 controls, good cycles 12 stops and
returns to the first field.
It is declared LAST, deliberately. `rules:gate` refused the entry when it was written first,
because no capture carried a `focusOrder` -- 'an entry that matches nothing enforces nothing'.
The probe reached the manifest through three separate hops that each enumerate case fields by
hand, and it was dropped at the third, so the rule shipped against zero evidence for as long as
the flag was silently false. Order of operations: capture the evidence, prove the signal
discriminates, then declare the owner.
A control the page ANNOUNCES as operable that Tab never reaches — the failure a screen-reader user
meets as 'I can hear it and I cannot press it'. Deterministic: two captured sequences compared.
POSITIONAL, because the focus probe truncates. Every corpus page stops at 12 tab stops, so absence
from `focusOrder` alone usually means the probe stopped and a rule keyed on it would fire almost
everywhere. A control counts as unreachable only when something LATER in reading order was reached.
Not the roleless `<div onclick>` of the custom-control family: that one is invisible to the screen
reader, which is its 4.1.2 finding, and a capture cannot tell it from a page with no button at all.
PARTIAL, and the part is the only one that is ours. A skip link is NOT required — W3C is explicit
that headings alone (H69) and landmarks alone (ARIA11) satisfy 2.4.1 — so detecting absence would
fire on conformant pages, and whether any mechanism EXISTS is a DOM fact the static layer answers
better than our nondeterministic landmark sweep.
This rule fires only on a mechanism that is present and inert: activating the skip link left focus
exactly where the next Tab would have gone anyway. Measured on the pair, which differ only in the
target id — 'Search the archive, edit' against 'News and updates, link'.
It requires the activated control to BE a skip link by name, because the probe takes the first link
on the page and on a real site that is as likely to be a logo.
Deterministic because the evidence is a comparison, not a reading: the first heading changed and
the title did not. Both come from the screen reader — `reportTitle` is the same command that fills
`documentReady.title`, so this is what a user hears when they ask where they are.
It covers ONE of 2.4.2's failure modes and deliberately not the others. A missing title is not
worth a rule (zero across 4,895 captures, and absent from the failures covering 96% of WebAIM's
million-page survey), and whether a title DESCRIBES its topic is judgement — W3C flags 2.4.2 on a
page titled 'Welcome to CityLights! [Inaccessible Survey Page]'. So this is partial coverage of the
criterion, and the part a screen reader is uniquely placed to prove: a static analyser cannot see
it at all, because the markup is valid at every instant and the failure is the transition.
The corroborating signal was chosen against a measurement rather than by reasoning. 'Nothing was
announced' is the obvious one and would never have fired: the failing page announced 'visited',
NVDA reporting the link's own state.
Deterministic because it is a comparison between two sequences the capture already holds: what the
page READS (structure.formFields) against what Tab VISITS (interaction.focusOrder). No judgement
enters it.
PARTIAL coverage, and the boundary is honest: whether an order 'preserves meaning' in general is
human judgement, the same wall 2.4.6 stops at. What is not a judgement call is a tab sequence that
contradicts the reading sequence for the same controls.
Only a screen reader can make this comparison. A static checker can flag tabindex="1" as a smell,
but the DOM has no reading order to contradict — that order only exists once something has walked
the page.
The rules cover a deliberate SUBSET and the scorer's head owns the rest, so neither 'rules' nor
silence is true. VAGUE_LINK_NAMES is six phrases chosen to be the ones context cannot rescue;
the corpus generates its link text from a wider vocabulary, so the rules fire on part of it.
This was invisible before: the old gate filtered to the two criteria it already believed the
rules owned, so a rule firing on any OTHER criterion could not be seen at all. Declaring the
overlap is what makes it visible; the gate asserts it stays a strict, non-empty subset, so
widening the vocabulary to everything (or breaking the rule to nothing) both fail.

4.1.2:state-change-silent.note: MOVED from the model on 2026-08-24, reversing a decision made on accuracy alone. The model scored 59/0/0 and a deterministic rule had been written and measured at 69/69 EXACT with no false positives across 1,001 conformant records -- so a rule looked redundant. It is not, because the two layers differ in what they may CLAIM, not only in how often they are right: a model finding carries no `mapping`, which means `secondary`, which `criterionOutcomes` reports as `cantTell`. A rule may be conformance-mapped and assert. `compare-layers.mjs` names this exact criterion as the difference between this tool and a static scanner -- axe can see that `aria-expanded` exists and cannot see that it never changes -- so the one finding nothing else can make was being reported as a maybe. Re-measured on the whole corpus after the move: 69 true positives, 0 false positives, 0 false negatives across 144 captures carrying state evidence.

note: Deterministic, and gated on the AX tree CONFIRMING zero headings rather than on the sweep finding
none -- a sweep alone cannot tell 'this page has none' from 'we could not ask'. That makes it a
rule and not a judgement, the same move ADR 0021 made for 4.1.2:state-change-silent.
Added 2026-08-26 with the five `headings-none-*` cases. Before them the rule was UNTESTABLE: page()
emitted an <h1> unconditionally, so across 2,366 records the count with zero headings was 0 and
rules:coverage read 'NEVER FIRED ANYWHERE -- the claim rests on nothing'.

3.3.3:error-remedy-missing.note: 3.3.3 since 2026-09-02, and it is rules-owned because a head DEMONSTRABLY could not learn it: recall 0.0 on its own training data under both poolings, with false positives on conformant records (known-gaps.md §22). The distinction is one clause inside a long announcement -- "Enter the visit date as DD slash MM slash YYYY" against "Invalid entry" -- which a document average dilutes and an instance max did not rescue. It does not need a head: whether the announced error contains an INSTRUCTION is read directly, which is this project's own test for what a rule may assert, and the same basis on which 1.1.1:filename-alt is rules-owned. The signal discriminated 44 captured pairs with no errors while the head could not fit 15. Like 3.3.1 and 4.1.3 it reads probe-gated channels, so it cannot fire on a real page -- probeForms is off for pages we do not own. NOT in MODEL_EXCLUDED_SUBTYPES, and the distinction cost a chain run to learn: `unavailable` means the records are EXCLUDED from the export because the evidence cannot express the failure, and `assert_declaration_matches_data` fails if a declared subtype has no records. Here the evidence expresses it exactly -- that is why a rule can assert from it -- so the records stay and RULE_SUBSTITUTED_SUBTYPES makes the head non-blocking instead. Declaring `rules` and excluding the records at the same time is a contradiction the trainer catches by name.

3.2.1:focus-context-change.note: 3.2.1 since 2026-09-02. Rules-owned because whether the page renamed itself between two reads is READ, not judged: focusing a control either changed the title or it did not, with no wording to interpret and no threshold to calibrate. Same basis as 3.3.3 and 1.1.1:filename-alt. NOT in MODEL_EXCLUDED_SUBTYPES: the evidence expresses the failure exactly, so the records stay and RULE_SUBSTITUTED_SUBTYPES makes the head non-blocking — declaring `rules` while excluding the records is the contradiction `assert_declaration_matches_data` catches by name.

3.2.2:input-context-change.note: 3.2.2 since 2026-09-02. Rules-owned because whether the page renamed itself between two reads is READ, not judged: typing into a control either changed the title or it did not, with no wording to interpret and no threshold to calibrate. Same basis as 3.3.3 and 1.1.1:filename-alt. NOT in MODEL_EXCLUDED_SUBTYPES: the evidence expresses the failure exactly, so the records stay and RULE_SUBSTITUTED_SUBTYPES makes the head non-blocking — declaring `rules` while excluding the records is the contradiction `assert_declaration_matches_data` catches by name.

note: NOBODY decides this one, and the held-out set is what established it rather than an argument.
The corpus pair is clean: both variants carry the SAME foreign passage and only the `lang` differs,
so the GOOD page makes NVDA announce the language and the BAD page produces silence. 29 cases, and
`check-signals` discriminates all of them. The head fitted them and then scored FOUR HELD-OUT
languages at 0.506, 0.513, 0.536 and 0.604 against a 0.979 cut -- eight false negatives, every one
of them a page whose only novelty is that the language is Dutch, Portuguese, Polish or Norwegian
rather than French, German, Italian or Spanish.
THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it is `3.3.2:placeholder-only`'s exactly. The corpus can express
the property because it KNOWS what it wrote; the screen reader cannot hear it. On the failing page
NVDA reads French with an English voice and says nothing about it -- so the evidence of the failure
is an ABSENCE, and a head detects a positive pattern in an announcement. There is no announcement to
detect. What it fitted instead was the corpus's four language names, which is why unseen ones sit at
chance.
Choosing DIFFERENT languages for the held-out set is what made this visible. Reusing the corpus's
would have measured memorisation and reported it as generalisation -- and the gate would have passed.
A RULE cannot decide it either, for the reason known-gaps SS36 sets out: an announcement CONFIRMS a
passage was marked, but silence is equally what a correct monolingual page produces, so accusing an
UNMARKED passage needs the language of the TEXT. That is language detection and the DOM's territory.
So neither layer here can, which is what `criterion-coverage.ts` already records as `reachable`
rather than `assessed`.
The 29 corpus cases STAY. They are ground truth for a future join against a DOM language census, and
they are what proved `[speech] reportLanguage` puts the language into the transcript at all.
